# Lecture 38.1: Path Space

## Introduction and the Path Space Framework

Given a totally ordered index set $T$ with least element $0$, an initial probability measure $\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S, \mathcal{B})$, and a family of Markov transition operators $\{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}$ satisfying the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations on a standard Borel space $(S, \mathcal{B})$ (@thm-canonical-markov-construction, Lecture 37.2), the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem constructs a canonical probability measure $\mathbb{P}^\nu \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$ on the infinite product space $S^T = \{\omega : T \to S\}$. Under $\mathbb{P}^\nu$, the coordinate process $X_t(\omega) = \omega(t)$ is a Markov process matching the specified finite-dimensional distributions.

However, not every Markov process associated with the data $(\nu, \{Q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t})$ "is" literally this coordinate process on $S^T$. In general, any stochastic process $X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}$ defined on an arbitrary probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ induces a pushforward measure $P_X$ on the path space $(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$:

::: {#def-law-of-process}
## Law of a Stochastic Process / Path Measure
Let $X = \{X_t\}_{t \in T}$ be an $S$-valued stochastic process defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$. The **law of the process** $X$, denoted by $P_X \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$, is the pushforward measure under the path map $\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto X_t(\omega))$:
$$
P_X(E) := \mathbb{P} \Big( \big\{ \omega \in \Omega : (t \mapsto X_t(\omega))_{t \in T} \in E \big\} \Big) \quad \text{for } E \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}.
$$ {#eq-law-of-process}
This is well defined: since $\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T} = \sigma(\pi_t : t \in T)$ and $\pi_t \circ (t \mapsto X_t(\omega)) = X_t$ is $(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{B})$-measurable for every $t \in T$, the path map $\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto X_t(\omega))$ is $(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$-measurable, so $P_X$ is a genuine probability measure on $(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$.
:::

---

## Limitations of the Product $\sigma$-Algebra
The product $\sigma$-algebra allows us to describe events determined by countably many coordinates, but it cannot capture every property of an entire path when the time index set is uncountable. A central measure-theoretic challenge arises when evaluating path properties (e.g., continuity, right-continuity, boundedness) directly on $(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$. 

::: {#rem-product-sigma-algebra-limitation}
## Smallness of $\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}$
Recall that the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T} := \sigma(\pi_t : t \in T)$ is generated by individual coordinate projections. Consequently (a standard fact about product $\sigma$-algebras, provable by a monotone-class argument: the collection of sets depending on only countably many coordinates is itself a $\sigma$-algebra containing every cylinder set, hence all of $\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}$), every set $E \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}$ depends on at most a **countable** subset of time coordinates $T_0 \subseteq T$, i.e. $E = \pi_{T_0}^{-1}(E')$ for some $E' \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T_0}$ and some countable $T_0 \subseteq T$.

When $T = [0, \infty)$, this countable-dependence property shows that path properties genuinely depending on uncountably many time coordinates are **not measurable** with respect to $\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}$. For example, the space of continuous paths $C([0, \infty), \mathbb{R})$ is **not** an element of $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})^{\otimes [0, \infty)}$: if it were, it would depend only on the coordinates in some countable $T_0 \subseteq [0,\infty)$, i.e. membership in $C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$ would be determined by $(\omega(t))_{t \in T_0}$ alone. But any $\omega \in C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$ can be modified at a single point $t^* \notin T_0$ (which exists since $T_0$ is countable and $[0,\infty)$ is not) to destroy continuity at $t^*$ while leaving all $T_0$-coordinates unchanged — contradicting that membership in $C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$ depends only on $T_0$.
:::

---

## Construction of Continuous-Time Markov Processes

## Brownian Motion

::: {#def-brownian-motion}
## Standard Brownian Motion
An adapted stochastic process $B = \{B_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \ge 0}, \mathbb{P})$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

0. **Standard Start:** $B_0 = 0$ $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
1. **Independent Increments:** For all $0 \le s < t$, $B_t - B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_s$ (in the sense of @def-independent-increments, Lecture 37.1). (If $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}$ is the natural filtration $\mathcal{F}_t^B = \sigma(B_u : u \le t)$, this is equivalent, via @rem-independent-increments-equivalent together with $B_0 = 0$, to the weaker-looking statement that for any $0 \le t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n$ the increments $B_{t_1}-B_{t_0},\dots,B_{t_n}-B_{t_{n-1}}$ are mutually independent; for a general, possibly strictly larger, filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}$ the two need not coincide, and it is independence from $\mathcal{F}_s$ that is required for the Markov property.)
2. **Gaussian Increments:** $B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t-s)$ for all $0 \le s < t$.
3. **Continuous Sample Paths:** The map $t \mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
:::

Using Kolmogorov's Extension Theorem, one can readily construct a Markov process $X = \{X_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ satisfying conditions (0)–(2) via the Gaussian transition kernel
$$
q_{s,t}(x, B) := \int_B \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(t-s)}} \exp \left( -\frac{(y-x)^2}{2(t-s)} \right) dy, 
$$ {#eq-bm-kernel}
for $0 \le s \le t$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$
together with $\nu = \delta_0$ as initial law, applying @thm-canonical-markov-construction (Lecture 37.2). Once a process $B$ with this law is in hand, @eq-bm-kernel indeed coincides with 
$$
q_{s,t}(x,B) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_B(x+B_t-B_s)]= \mathbb{P}(x + B_t - B_s \in B),
$$ 
since $x + B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(x,\, t-s)$.

The corresponding transition operators $Q_{s,t} f = \gamma_{t-s} * f$ (where $\gamma_\tau$ denotes the centered Gaussian density with variance $\tau$) satisfy the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations by convolution properties of independent normal distributions:
$$
\gamma_{s-r} * \gamma_{t-s} = \gamma_{t-r}, \quad \text{which gives} \quad Q_{r,s} Q_{s,t} = Q_{r,t}.
$$ {#eq-bm-ck-convolution}

Moreover, because the kernel is translation-invariant ($q_{s,t}(x,\cdot)$ is the law of $x + Z_{s,t}$ for $Z_{s,t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,t-s)$ not depending on $x$ beyond this translation), the resulting finite-dimensional law of $(X_{t_0}, X_{t_1}, \dots, X_{t_n})$ factors, via the change of variables $z_i = x_i - x_{i-1}$ (exactly as in the arrival-time computation of @prp-poisson-arrival-characterization below), into a product of the marginal law of $X_{t_0}$ and independent $\mathcal{N}(0, t_i - t_{i-1})$ laws for the increments $z_i = X_{t_i}-X_{t_{i-1}}$. This confirms that $X$ constructed this way indeed also satisfies condition (1), i.e. has independent increments relative to its own natural filtration.


Property 3 asserts that the sample paths of $B$ are continuous almost surely:
$$
\mathbb{P}\!\Big(\big\{\omega \in \Omega : t \mapsto B_t(\omega) \text{ is continuous on } [0,\infty)\big\}\Big) = 1.
$$
Equivalently, there exists $\Omega' \in \mathcal{F}$ with $\mathbb{P}(\Omega') = 1$ such that for every $\omega \in \Omega'$ and every $t_0 \ge 0$, $\lim_{t \to t_0} B_t(\omega) = B_{t_0}(\omega)$.

For this statement to make sense, the set $\{\omega : t \mapsto B_t(\omega) \text{ is continuous}\}$ must belong to $\mathcal{F}$. This is where the lecture’s remark bites: the set of continuous paths $C([0,\infty), \mathbb{R})$ is not a member of the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})^{\otimes [0,\infty)}$, as shown there — continuity genuinely depends on uncountably many coordinates simultaneously, so it lies outside what the product $\sigma$-algebra can see.

However, incorporating **path continuity** (Property 3) requires substantial further analysis (e.g., Kolmogorov's Continuity Theorem or explicit series expansions). An explicit constructive representation using i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ random variables $\{\xi_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$ on $t \in [0, 1]$ is given by the Paley–Wiener / Fourier series:
$$
B_t = \xi_0 \, t + \sqrt{2} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \xi_n \, \frac{\sin(n \pi t)}{n \pi}, \qquad t \in [0,1],
$$
(or standard Haar/Lévy–Ciesielski series expansions), where the series converges uniformly in $t$ almost surely, which is what yields the a.s. continuity of $t \mapsto B_t$.

---

## The Poisson Process and Jump Timings

::: {#def-poisson-process}
## Poisson Process
An adapted process $N = \{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \ge 0}, \mathbb{P})$ and taking values in $\mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ is a **Poisson process** with rate $\lambda > 0$ if:

0. **Standard Start:** $N_0 = 0$ $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
1. **Independent Increments:** For all $0 \le s < t$, $N_t - N_s$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_s$; equivalently (given $N_0=0$), increments over disjoint intervals are mutually independent.
2. **Poisson Increments:** $N_t - N_s \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))$ for all $0 \le s < t$.
3. **Cadlag / Right-Continuous Paths:** $t \mapsto N_t(\omega)$ is non-decreasing and right-continuous $\mathbb{P}$-a.s., with jumps of size exactly $1$.
:::

Property 3 is not redundant: it is a genuine regularity condition on sample paths that is **not** implied by properties 0–2 alone (@rem-path-property-warning below spells this out), and it is exactly what makes $N$ a bona fide counting process whose jump times can be read off from the path. (That the jumps automatically have size $1$, given right-continuity and monotonicity, follows from $\mathbb{P}(N_{t+h}-N_t \ge 2) = O(h^2)$ as $h \downarrow 0$ together with a standard dyadic-partition/Borel–Cantelli argument; we take it as part of the definition here rather than re-derive it.)

We explicitly construct $N_t$ from jump arrival times $X_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \xi_k$ (with $X_0 := 0$), where $\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^\infty \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda)$:
$$
N_t(\omega) := \sup \left\{ n \in \mathbb{N}_0 : X_n(\omega) \le t \right\}.
$$ {#eq-poisson-explicit-def}

The transition kernel on the discrete state space $S = \mathbb{N}_0$ is given by:
$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{s,t}(n, m) &= \mathbb{P}(n + N_t - N_s = m)\\
& = e^{-\lambda(t-s)} \frac{\big(\lambda(t-s)\big)^{m-n}}{(m-n)!} \quad \text{for } m \ge n.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-poisson-kernel}

Convolution of independent Poisson variables confirms that $\{q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}$ satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations.

::: {#prp-poisson-arrival-characterization}
## Characterization of Jump Times
Let $N = \{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ satisfy properties (0)–(3) of @def-poisson-process (so, in particular, $N_0 = 0$ a.s. and $N$ has non-decreasing, right-continuous paths with unit jumps, in addition to independent and Poisson increments). Define the sequence of jump arrival times by $X_n := \inf \{ t \ge 0 : N_t = n\}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, and the inter-arrival times $\xi_n := X_n - X_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$. Then $\{\xi_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ are i.i.d. $\text{Exp}(\lambda)$ random variables.

(Properties 0 and 3 are essential, not merely convenient: they are what make $X_n$ the literal $n$-th jump time of the path $t \mapsto N_t(\omega)$, so that $\{X_n \in J_n\}$ can be read off from the values of $N$ at the endpoints of $J_n$. Properties (1)–(2) alone, without path regularity, do **not** suffice for this conclusion — see @rem-path-property-warning.)
:::

::: {#prf-poisson-arrival-characterization}
## Proof
Fix $n \ge 1$. Partition $[0, t_n]$ into alternating disjoint intervals:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&K_1 = (0, s_1], \; J_1 = (s_1, t_1], \; K_2 = (t_1, s_2], \; J_2 = (s_2, t_2],\\
& \dots, \; K_n = (t_{n-1}, s_n], \; J_n = (s_n, t_n],
\end{aligned}
$$
where $0 < s_1 < t_1 < s_2 < t_2 < \dots < s_n < t_n$. Denote $N(s, t) := N_t - N_s$.

Since $N_0 = 0$ and $N$ is non-decreasing, right-continuous, with unit jumps (property 3), the path $t\mapsto N_t(\omega)$ passes through every integer value it ever reaches, one at a time, so for each $n$ there is a.s. a well-defined, finite, strictly increasing sequence of jump times $X_1(\omega) < X_2(\omega) < \dots$ with $N_t(\omega) = \#\{k \ge 1 : X_k(\omega) \le t\}$. In particular, $X_j \in (s_j, t_j]$ holds if and only if no jump has occurred by time $s_j$ beyond the $(j-1)$-th (i.e. $N_{s_j} \le j-1$) and the $j$-th jump has occurred by time $t_j$ (i.e. $N_{t_j} \ge j$); this is what licenses translating the event $\{X_1 \in J_1, \dots, X_n \in J_n\}$ into the disjoint increment conditions below. The event $\{X_1 \in J_1, X_2 \in J_2, \dots, X_n \in J_n\}$ corresponds to:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\{X_1 \in J_1, \dots, X_n \in J_n\} \\
&= \left\{ \bigcap_{j=1}^n \{N(K_j) = 0\} \right\} \cap \left\{ \bigcap_{j=1}^{n-1} \{N(J_j) = 1\} \right\} \cap \{N(J_n) \ge 1\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-event-decomposition}

Because $N$ has independent increments over disjoint intervals $K_1, J_1, \dots, K_n, J_n$, these $2n$ events are independent. Recalling that $\mathbb{P}(N(J) = k) = e^{-\lambda|J|} \frac{(\lambda|J|)^k}{k!}$ and $\mathbb{P}(N(J) \ge 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda|J|}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_1 \in J_1, \dots, X_n \in J_n) &= \left( \prod_{j=1}^n e^{-\lambda |K_j|} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} \lambda |J_j| e^{-\lambda |J_j|} \right) \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda |J_n|} \right) \\
&= \lambda^{n-1} \left( \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} |J_j| \right) e^{-\lambda s_n} \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda(t_n - s_n)} \right) \\
&= \lambda^{n-1} \left( \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} |J_j| \right) \left( e^{-\lambda s_n} - e^{-\lambda t_n} \right) \\
&= \int_{J_1} \dots \int_{J_n} \lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n} \, dx_1 dx_2 \dots dx_n.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-poisson-density-integral}

By Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ Theorem, the joint distribution of $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ on $\Delta_n = \{0 < x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_n\}$ has joint density:
$$
f_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda x_n} \mathbf{1}_{\{0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n\}}.
$$ {#eq-joint-density-x}

Applying the change of variables transformation $\xi_k = X_k - X_{k-1}$ (with $X_0 = 0$), the Jacobian determinant is $1$, yielding joint density:
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n}(u_1, \dots, u_n) &= \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum_{k=1}^n u_k} \mathbf{1}_{\{u_1 > 0, \dots, u_n > 0\}} \\
&= \prod_{k=1}^n \left( \lambda e^{-\lambda u_k} \mathbf{1}_{\{u_k > 0\}} \right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-joint-density-xi}

This proves that $\{\xi_k\}_{k=1}^n$ are i.i.d. $\text{Exp}(\lambda)$ random variables. $\blacksquare$
:::

---

## Insufficiency of Transition Kernels for Path Properties

::: {#rem-path-property-warning}
## Moral: Path Properties Lie Outside Transition Kernels
Property 3 (right-continuity of $t \mapsto N_t$) **does not** follow from the finite-dimensional distributions or transition kernels alone — nor, as noted above, does it follow from properties (0)–(2).

To demonstrate this, consider the modified process defined using the **arrival times** $X_n$ (not the inter-arrival times $\xi_n$):
$$
M_t(\omega) := \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{[0, t)}(X_n(\omega)) = N_{t-}(\omega).
$$ {#eq-modified-process}
Because each $X_n$ has a continuous (atomless) law, $\mathbb{P}(X_n = t) = 0$ for every fixed $t \ge 0$, so $\mathbb{P}(M_t \ne N_t) = 0$ at each fixed $t$, and in fact $\mathbb{P}(M_{t_1} \ne N_{t_1}, \dots, \text{or } M_{t_k} \ne N_{t_k}) = 0$ for every finite set of times $t_1, \dots, t_k$ (a finite union of null events is null). Hence $\{M_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ has the exact same finite-dimensional distributions as $\{N_t\}_{t \ge 0}$, but its paths are **left-continuous** instead of right-continuous (it is the left-limit process $N_{t-}$).

**Key Takeaway:** Transition kernels $\{q_{s,t}\}_{s \le t}$ uniquely specify finite-dimensional distributions on $(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$, but they **do not dictate sample path properties** (such as continuity, cadlag paths, or measurability of path functionals). Sample path regularity requires selecting an appropriate separable modification or constructing the process on a restricted path space (such as $D([0, \infty), S)$ or $C([0, \infty), S)$).
:::

---

## Takeaways

- **Law of a process vs. the canonical coordinate process.** Any stochastic process $X$ on an arbitrary probability space has a well-defined law $P_X \in \mathcal{P}(S^T, \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T})$ (@def-law-of-process), but $X$ need not literally be the coordinate process constructed by the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem — the two share only their finite-dimensional distributions.
- **The product $\sigma$-algebra is too small for path properties.** Every $E \in \mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}$ depends on only countably many coordinates (@rem-product-sigma-algebra-limitation), so for $T = [0,\infty)$, sets like $C([0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$ that genuinely depend on uncountably many coordinates are not $\mathcal{B}^{\otimes T}$-measurable at all.
- **Brownian motion and the Poisson process as Markov processes built from the KET.** Both are specified by an initial law together with a transition kernel (Gaussian, resp. Poisson), which is readily checked to satisfy Chapman–Kolmogorov; the Kolmogorov Extension Theorem then produces a process with the correct finite-dimensional distributions, including independent increments and (for a Markov process with a translation-invariant kernel) the correct marginal law of each increment. What the KET construction does **not** automatically provide is path regularity (continuity for BM, cadlag unit-jump paths for the Poisson process) — these are additional facts (Kolmogorov's continuity theorem, explicit series or renewal constructions) that must be established separately, and that require $N_0 = 0$ (resp. $B_0 = 0$) to even be meaningful.
- **The arrival-time characterization genuinely needs path regularity.** Showing that the jump times of a Poisson process have i.i.d. $\text{Exp}(\lambda)$ increments (@prp-poisson-arrival-characterization) requires not just independent Poisson increments but also that $N$ has non-decreasing, right-continuous, unit-jump paths starting at $0$ — without this, the hitting times $X_n = \inf\{t : N_t = n\}$ need not correspond to literal jump times of the path.
- **Moral: transition kernels do not determine sample path properties.** Two processes with identical finite-dimensional distributions (e.g. $N$ and its left-continuous modification $M = N_{-}$) can have incompatible path properties (right- vs. left-continuity); selecting a version with the "correct" regularity is a separate construction, not a consequence of the finite-dimensional distributions (@rem-path-property-warning).
